article.title: Aeon vs Claude Duet: the agent that asks and the one that runs

note_tweet.text:
Imagine giving an AI system one instruction before going to sleep:

"Find a genuine business problem, investigate the market, and build a working solution for under $15."

By morning, it has identified a promising opportunity, analyzed competitors, created a functional prototype, and prepared a launch plan.

You can build parts of this workflow today.

But connecting six powerful AI tools doesn't automatically create a profitable business.

The real challenge is making each tool responsible for something it can actually do.

Here's how I'd design the system.

FIND PROBLEMS PEOPLE ARE ALREADY DISCUSSING

Start with Grok and its X Search capabilities.

Ask it to investigate recent discussions about a particular industry.

For example:

"Find recurring complaints from independent delivery drivers about income tracking, payment reconciliation, and managing earnings across multiple platforms.

Group similar complaints, identify recurring problems, and provide the original sources."

Instead of collecting random startup ideas, you're investigating problems people are actively experiencing.

But don't confuse 1,000 complaints with 1,000 potential customers.

Remove duplicates, distinguish individual users from repeated posts, and look for evidence that people are actively seeking solutions.

CHECK WHETHER THE OPPORTUNITY IS REAL

This is where I'd introduce Jev.

Jev is a structured AI decision model developed by TypeSafe AI.

It can evaluate specific questions and return structured results that software can use.

For example:

Does this problem affect the target customer?

Is there evidence of existing demand?

Does the proposed solution address the actual complaint?

Is the available evidence sufficient to justify further research?

Your application can combine these evaluations using predefined scoring rules.

But here's the improvement.

Don't allow Jev to decide that a business will be profitable.

Use it to prioritize opportunities for further investigation.

Actual demand needs external evidence.

LET CLAUDE OPUS DESIGN THE SOLUTION

Once an opportunity passes the initial screening, give Claude Opus 5.5 the research findings.

Ask it to prepare:

A precise problem statement.

The target customer profile.

An analysis of existing alternatives.

A minimum viable product specification.

The simplest viable technology stack.

A realistic development and operating budget.

I'd also ask Claude to identify the strongest reason the product might fail.

A good AI business adviser should challenge the idea before development begins.

USE CODING AGENTS TO BUILD THE PROTOTYPE

This is where Claude Code or Codex becomes useful.

Imagine the chosen opportunity is an income tracker for delivery drivers.

Instead of immediately building a complex financial platform, start with three functions:

Import earnings from CSV files.

Calculate income across platforms.

Display weekly earnings and expenses.

Use a simple framework such as Next.js with SQLite or another suitable database.

Keep the first version small enough to verify.

The coding agent can implement features, execute tests, investigate errors, and prepare deployment.

But require passing tests and a working preview before accepting the result.

And don't automatically purchase domains, activate paid infrastructure, or publish software without authorization.

USE REA ONLY WHEN IT ADDS REAL VALUE

Reverse Engineer Anything (REA) is useful for investigating software behavior and implementation details.

It isn't a replacement for market research.

If you need to understand how an application you're authorized to examine implements a particular feature, REA can help collect technical evidence.

For ordinary competitor pricing, positioning, reviews, and customer complaints, conventional research tools are more appropriate.

Don't add a powerful tool merely because it exists.

CONNECT EVERYTHING THROUGH A CONTROLLED WORKFLOW

This is where an orchestration layer matters.

ChatGPT Dots can manage ongoing responsibilities and delegate supported work, subject to availability, connected tools, and permissions.

Alternatively, n8n or a custom Python workflow can provide more explicit control over scheduling, API calls, approval gates, and execution state.

I'd use a workflow like this:

Market Monitoring
→ Problem Discovery
→ Evidence Collection
→ Opportunity Qualification
→ Product Specification
→ Prototype Development
→ Automated Testing
→ Human Approval
→ Controlled Launch
Each stage produces a documented result before the next begins.
Obsidian can serve as the knowledge archive, storing research, decisions, product specifications, and experiment results.
But automatic recordkeeping requires an integration that actually writes those records. Simply installing Obsidian doesn't create an audit trail.
VERIFY THE BUSINESS RESULTS
This is the part I'd never automate away.
Suppose your AI system identifies 243 interested users and 31 purchase a $9 monthly subscription.
That's $279 in monthly recurring revenue, assuming all 31 subscriptions are active.
Not $832.

And even that isn't necessarily profit.

You still need to account for payment processing, hosting, API usage, refunds, and customer acquisition.

A successful overnight launch should be measured through verified transactions and genuine user activity.

Not registrations alone.

THE MOST IMPORTANT IMPROVEMENT

I'd divide the entire system into three responsibilities.

AI investigates opportunities and develops possible solutions.

Deterministic software enforces budgets, validates outputs, and manages execution.

Humans approve spending, external communication, and public launches.

This prevents a promising autonomous workflow from becoming an expensive chain of uncontrolled actions.

And here's the bigger opportunity.

You don't necessarily need six AI platforms working together.

You need the smallest combination capable of repeatedly producing useful, verifiable results.

Start with one industry.

Identify one problem.

Build one functional prototype.

Test it with actual potential customers.

Then automate the parts that prove valuable.

The future of autonomous AI entrepreneurship isn't simply launching hundreds of products overnight.

It's reducing the time and cost required to discover whether a business idea deserves to exist.

That's where AI agents can create a genuine competitive advantage.

Here’s what I’ve had my @ChatGPT  Dots help me with over the past two weeks. Too much so I ask dots to pick some, besides coding and research:

1）Organize daycare updates
Save daily meals, naps, activities, and photos to Craft. When photos fail to download or go missing, go back, fill in the gaps, and check that they actually show up.

2）Keep a daily work log
Track what’s done, what’s still in progress, and what’s waiting on a reply. Save it to Craft and update the records when I give it new information. No digging through old chats myself.

3）Filter physical mail
Actually look at USPS envelope previews, check who they’re addressed to, and filter out ads and mail for previous residents. Flag the tax, insurance, and DMV letters worth paying attention to.

4）Find deals and place orders
Compare places to buy Stelo, find a better deal with a discount, and place the order. Also track gift card cashback for brands like Starbucks and Target, and only ping me when there’s a new increase.

5）Handle returns, refunds, and subscriptions
Chat with Amazon and the NEMIX seller to sort out conflicting return instructions and get free return shipping confirmed in writing. Follow up on an OWC refund. Contact GNC and cross-check the records to find that a refund had already arrived. Cancel unwanted Blue Bottle and Amazon subscriptions.

6）Deal with app support
Dots notifications, Bartender menu bar issues, Exist tags, Bevel chat glitches, Claude folder permissions. Put together reproduction steps, submit reports, answer follow-up questions, and track replies. Saves me from explaining the same problem over and over.

7）Troubleshoot health data syncing
Help work through sync failures, missing Apple Health writes, and duplicate records across Stelo and Bevel. Follow up on support replies until I confirmed health data was writing again.

8）Prepare tax mailings
Check documents and mailing addresses, prepare shipping labels, and sort out the post office steps, postmarks, and receipts before I go.

9）Organize appointment notes and recordings
File visit records, combine notes, and add follow-ups to the calendar. Find the relevant part of a recording and cut out a short clip so I can listen to it directly.

10）Reschedule appointments
Find available slots, move two Quest appointments together, replace the old bookings, and check the calendar updates. Actually make the change, not just send me a booking link.

11）Organize insurance renewal paperwork
Download official notices, file them, and turn the renewal process into specific tasks with dates: documents, information checks, submission, and follow-up.

12）File daycare bills
Find the MyProcare PDFs, rename them by month, save them to the right Dropbox folder, check the files, and close the Todoist task.

13）Fix the wine cellar connection
Identify the wrong integration, remove it, keep the correct one, and verify that it can actually read my inventory. (wine inventory is built by dots too)

@thsottiaux the only important thing is one dot is not enough, too much inside one. Dots has s at end, when can we see more dots in one account?

OpenAI dots
→ run on GPT-6 Astra with a browser

→ follow written rules: allow, ask first, or block each action

━━━━━━━━━━

Grok Bot
→ one computer per bot, running 24/7
→ hidden router, no model to pick

Show it a workflow once, it saves the routine.
A Chief of Staff bot hands work to the others.

━━━━━━━━━━

Jev · the gate

you → agent → Jev → app

Every send, refund or delete passes Jev first.
→ answers in 70 to 500 ms
→ picks from up to 255 options
→ attaches a probability
→ $0.042 per 1M input, output free

The math:
300K decisions a month
× 2K input tokens each
= 600M tokens
= $25.20 a month

That's the price of asking before every action.

→ first dot is included, start there

Your apps have no clean API?
→ add Grok Bot

Either way?
→ Jev goes in front of anything that moves money or deletes something

→ $25.20 is the infographic's own assumption
